title: Standard Input, Output, and Error knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which topic is explicitly listed under “Standard Input, Output, and Error”?
questions.explanation: The supplied Bash.pdf curriculum lists “Standard input ( stdin )” under lesson 16, “Standard Input, Output, and Error”. Review the topic in the lesson content to connect the term with its practical use.

questions.prompt: Which approach is the strongest default when applying “Standard Input, Output, and Error”?
options: Assume that a working happy-path example proves correctness for every input.
Evaluate constructed user-controlled strings as shell commands to reduce parsing code.
Skip version checks because all common environments provide the same Bash features.
Use commands and arguments deliberately, and inspect stdout, stderr, and the exit status separately.
questions.answer_key: Use commands and arguments deliberately, and inspect stdout, stderr, and the exit status separately.
questions.explanation: Use commands and arguments deliberately, and inspect stdout, stderr, and the exit status separately. This approach keeps assumptions visible and makes results verifiable.

questions.prompt: Which practice best prevents a common reliability or maintenance error related to “Standard Input, Output, and Error”?
options: Skip invalid inputs because the example uses trusted sample data.
Treat one successful output as proof that the workflow is safe in production.
Check the relevant command statuses immediately and report failures instead of inferring success from output.
Assume the command behaves the same across all versions and operating systems.
questions.answer_key: Check the relevant command statuses immediately and report failures instead of inferring success from output.
questions.explanation: Check the relevant command statuses immediately and report failures instead of inferring success from output. The appropriate checks depend on the target environment and should be reviewed before publishing a script.
